title: The space inside the pot
hookLine: an empty clay pot holds a little piece of sky. Gaudapada asks what happens to that sky when the pot breaks
carry: atman is like space: one, never cut apart
last: THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: A BLADE OF GRASS AND THE OCEAN.

lines: AN EMPTY POT ON A SHELF.
A PIECE OF THE SAME SPACE.
THE POT BREAKS. WHERE DID IT GO?
cards: An empty clay pot sits on a kitchen shelf. Empty, we say. But inside it is space, a small round piece of the same open space that fills the kitchen, the street, the sky over the house.
Pour water in and the water takes up that space. Pour it out and the space is still there, shaped like the pot. Now drop the pot.
It shatters. Where did the space inside it go? It didn't fly anywhere.
It didn't break. It just stopped looking separate. Gaudapada uses exactly this picture in the Mandukya Karika.

teach.b: In the Karika's section called Advaita, not-two, Gaudapada says the self, atman, is like space, and living beings, each of us, are like the space inside pots. The pots seem to make many small spaces out of one.
When the pots break, he says, the space in each merges back into space. So it is with living beings and the self.
Then he answers the obvious objection: if we're all one self, why does one person suffer while another is happy? His reply stays with the pots.

teach.h: SMOKE IN ONE POT, NOT IN ALL.
teach.b: If the space in one pot is filled with dust and smoke, the space in every other pot isn't dirty. One person's joy or grief doesn't spill into all the others.
Forms differ, uses differ, names differ, he says, yet space itself is not divided. Other Vedanta schools read the self and living beings as truly distinct, and answer this image in their own way.

teach.h: NOT A PIECE, NOT A CHANGE.
teach.b: The space in the pot is not a piece cut out of space, and not something space turned into. Just so, a living being is not a part of the self or a change in it. Last: to children, he says, the sky can look dirty.

teach.h: THE DIRT IS IN THE SEEING.
teach.b: The dirt is in the seeing, not in the sky. So the self only seems stained to those who don't yet see clearly. The smoke drifts, the pot breaks, and the sky was never touched.
That's the Advaita teaching in one picture: one self in every being. And one self isn't one mood: your grief is still yours; the space it sits in isn't divided.

how: Students of Advaita Vedanta often read the Mandukya Karika with Shankara's commentary under a teacher, and the image of space in a pot is still used in talks and classes to point to the self.

smoke in one pot doesn't dirty the space in the others.

games.why: he stays with the pots: the dust and smoke in one don't stain the rest, and space itself is never divided.

practice: Look at a cup or a bowl near you and notice the space inside it, then the space around it, then the room's space running out through a window or a door.
Close your eyes if you like and rest in that openness; when a thought arrives, let it be smoke in one pot, which doesn't change the space. If you pray, you can rest there as an offering.

wordCard.voice: The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, where the self is pictured as open space, and each life as space held for a while inside a pot.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the space in a pot, from ghata, a pot, and akasha, space. The Karika's word for the image.

carryVoice: Your line: atman is like space: one, never cut apart. Smoke in one pot never stains the sky. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mandukya Karika 3.3–3.8 (the self like space; living beings like the space in pots; when pots break the spaces merge; smoke in one pot does not soil all; names and forms differ but space does not; neither part nor modification; the sky looks dirty to children)
